headline: Humble Mushrooms Offer Hope for Plastic, Housing, and Food
meta_description: From sustainable materials to food security, mushrooms are emerging as unexpected allies in solving the planet's most pressing challenges, experts say.
summary_short: On World Mushroom Day, researchers highlight how fungi are being used to replace plastic, create affordable housing, and fight food insecurity across Africa and beyond.
body:
Mushrooms may seem like a humble food, but they're quietly becoming part of the solution to some of humanity's biggest challenges. On World Mushroom Day (October 15), researchers and innovators are drawing attention to fungi's remarkable potential—from creating sustainable materials that could replace plastic and leather, to developing affordable protein sources for vulnerable communities, to supporting farmers with new income streams. According to Gabriela D'Elia, director of the Fungal Diversity Survey, projects worldwide are already harnessing mushrooms to address food security and waste management. One company, Evocative, uses a mushroom called artist's conk to create materials with applications in packaging and fashion. "Fungi are showing us new ways to live in allyship with the planet," D'Elia said.

In Nigeria, researchers have made a breakthrough by cultivating Lentinus squarrosulus—a wild mushroom with both culinary and medicinal value—using sawdust, an agricultural waste product. This domestication could transform farming across Africa by offering an inexpensive and reliable protein source in regions where it's needed most. The mushroom, which typically grows on decaying logs in tropical forests, faces extinction in the wild due to habitat destruction, making its cultivation especially urgent.

Not all mushroom news is encouraging, however. A 2025 study found that golden oyster mushrooms—prized edible fungi with bright yellow caps native to Asia—are becoming invasive in North American forests, displacing native fungal species. Researchers warn that cultivators must be mindful of where their mushrooms end up. Yet these cautionary tales underscore a larger truth: fungi deserve our attention, whether as food, medicine, material, or ecological indicator. The humble mushroom, it seems, has much to teach us.
quick_facts: October 15 is World Mushroom Day, celebrating fungi's multiple benefits
Evocative uses artist's conk mushroom to replace plastic and leather
Nigerian researchers grew Lentinus squarrosulus on sawdust waste
Golden oyster mushrooms are invasive in North American forests
Mushrooms provide food, medicine, housing materials, and income for farmers
